question.problem:
Find the equation of the **normal** line to the polar curve $r=\operatorname{sin}⁡(2\theta )$ at $\theta =\frac{3\pi }{4},$ given that 

$$
\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}=\frac{3\operatorname{sin}⁡(3\theta )-\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta }{3\operatorname{cos}⁡(3\theta )+\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta }.
$$
question.worked_solution:
To find the equation of the normal line to a polar curve at a point $P,$ we follow four steps:

**Step 1**: Calculate the derivative $\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}:$

In this case, we're given that

$$
\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}=\frac{3\operatorname{sin}⁡(3\theta )-\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta }{3\operatorname{cos}⁡(3\theta )+\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta }.
$$

**Step 2**: Find the slope of the tangent at $P:$

The slope of the tangent line is

$$
\begin{aligned}m & ={\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}|}_{\theta =3\pi /4} \\  & =\frac{(3\operatorname{sin}⁡(\frac{9\pi }{4})-\operatorname{sin}⁡(\frac{3\pi }{4}))}{(3\operatorname{cos}⁡(\frac{9\pi }{4})+\operatorname{cos}⁡(\frac{3\pi }{4}))} \\  & =\frac{(\frac{3\sqrt{2}}{2}-\frac{\sqrt{2}}{2})}{(\frac{3\sqrt{2}}{2}+(-\frac{\sqrt{2}}{2}))} \\  & =\frac{(\frac{2\sqrt{2}}{2})}{(\frac{2\sqrt{2}}{2})} \\  & =1.\end{aligned}
$$

**Step 3**: Find the Cartesian coordinates of $P:$

We compute the $xy$-coordinates of $P$ as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}{x}_{1} & =r\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta  \\  & =\operatorname{sin}⁡(2\theta )\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta  \\  & =\operatorname{sin}⁡(\frac{3\pi }{2})\operatorname{cos}⁡(\frac{3\pi }{4}) \\  & =(-1)\cdot (-\frac{\sqrt{2}}{2}) \\  & =\frac{\sqrt{2}}{2} \\ {y}_{1} & =r\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta  \\  & =\operatorname{sin}⁡(2\theta )\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta  \\  & =\operatorname{sin}⁡(\frac{3\pi }{2})\operatorname{sin}⁡(\frac{3\pi }{4}) \\  & =(-1)\cdot (\frac{\sqrt{2}}{2}) \\  & =-\frac{\sqrt{2}}{2}\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the coordinates of $P$ are $(\frac{\sqrt{2}}{2},-\frac{\sqrt{2}}{2}).$

**Step 4**: Using point-slope form, find the equation of the normal:

We find the equation of the normal as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}y-{y}_{1} & =-\frac{1}{m}(x-{x}_{1}) \\ y-(-\frac{\sqrt{2}}{2}) & =-1\cdot (x-\frac{\sqrt{2}}{2}) \\ y+\frac{\sqrt{2}}{2} & =-x+\frac{\sqrt{2}}{2} \\ y & =-x\end{aligned}
$$
